l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, HOMERICA / THE EXPEDITION OF AMPHIARAUS
s: Homer sat in a tanner’s yard and recited his poetry to those present. Among the works he recited was the Expedition of Amphiarus to Thebes. He also recited the Hymns to the Gods, which were composed by him.

l: Homer, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, HOMERICA / THE EXPEDITION OF AMPHIARAUS
s: Homer sat in a tanner’s yard and recited his poetry to those present. He had composed the Hymns to the Gods.

l: Expedition of Amphiarus to Thebes, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, HOMERICA / THE EXPEDITION OF AMPHIARAUS
s: The Expedition of Amphiarus to Thebes was one of the works Homer recited in the tanner’s yard.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE TAKING OF OECHALIA
s: The Taking of Oechalia concerns Eurytus, his daughter Iole, and Heracles, who sacked Oechalia for Iole's sake. The poem is attributed either to Homer or to Creophylus of Samos, who is said to have hosted Homer. Creophylus says that Eurytus had two sons, differing from Hesiod's account of four. The poem also preserves an account in which Medea poisoned Creon in Corinth, left her sons at the altar of Hera Acraea, and fled to Athens.

l: The Taking of Oechalia, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE TAKING OF OECHALIA
s: The Taking of Oechalia concerns Eurytus, his daughter Iole, and Heracles. It is attributed either to Homer or to Creophylus of Samos, and it also contains an account of Medea's actions in Corinth and Athens.

l: Oechalia, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE TAKING OF OECHALIA
s: Oechalia was sacked by Heracles for the sake of Iole.

l: Eurytus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE TAKING OF OECHALIA
s: Eurytus is described as the father of Iole, for whose sake Heracles sacked Oechalia. Creophylus says that Eurytus had two sons, while Hesiod says that he had four.

l: Iole, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE TAKING OF OECHALIA
s: Iole, also called Ioleia, was Eurytus's daughter. Heracles sacked Oechalia for her sake.

l: Heracles, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE TAKING OF OECHALIA
s: Heracles sacked Oechalia for the sake of Eurytus's daughter Iole.

l: Creophylus of Samos, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE TAKING OF OECHALIA
s: Creophylus of Samos is said to have hosted Homer and to have received the attribution of The Taking of Oechalia as a reward. Another account says that Creophylus wrote the poem and Homer lent it his name. Creophylus also says that Eurytus had two sons and gives an account of Medea's actions.

l: Homer, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE TAKING OF OECHALIA
s: Homer is associated with The Taking of Oechalia, although the poem's attribution is disputed. One account says that Homer gave the poem's attribution to Creophylus after being hosted by him; another says that Homer lent his name to Creophylus's poem.

l: Medea, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE TAKING OF OECHALIA
s: According to the account attributed to Creophylus, Medea poisoned Creon while living in Corinth. She then fled to Athens, leaving her young sons at the altar of Hera Acraea, while Creon's relatives killed them and spread the story that she had killed them and Creon.

l: Corinth, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE TAKING OF OECHALIA
s: Corinth was the city where Medea was living when she poisoned Creon, who ruled it at that time.

l: Creon, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE TAKING OF OECHALIA
s: Creon was the ruler of Corinth when Medea poisoned him. After his death, his relatives killed Medea's sons and spread the story that Medea had killed both them and Creon.

l: Athens, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE TAKING OF OECHALIA
s: Athens was the place to which Medea fled because she feared Creon's friends and relatives.

l: sacking of Oechalia, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE TAKING OF OECHALIA
s: The sacking of Oechalia was carried out by Heracles for the sake of Iole, the daughter of Eurytus.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE PHOCAIS
s: The unit concerns Homer’s composition of the Lesser Iliad and the Phocais. Pseudo-Herodotus states that Homer composed both works while living with Thestorides. The Phocaeans claim that Homer composed the Phocais among them.

l: Phocais, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE PHOCAIS
s: Homer composed the Phocais while living with Thestorides. The Phocaeans say that he composed it among them.

l: Homer, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE PHOCAIS
s: While living with Thestorides, Homer composed the Lesser Iliad and the Phocais.

l: The Little Iliad, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE PHOCAIS
s: The Lesser Iliad was composed by Homer while he was living with Thestorides.

l: Phocaeans, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE PHOCAIS
s: The Phocaeans say that Homer composed the Phocais among them.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE MARGITES
s: The unit concerns the Margites, which Suidas says was written by Pigres and attributed to Homer. It identifies Pigres as a Carian of Halicarnassus and brother of Artemisia, wife of Mausolus. The fragments describe Margites as a man who knew many things badly, lacked practical skills, and behaved foolishly toward his parents and wife. A proverb in the work contrasts the fox’s many tricks with the hedgehog’s single effective trick.

l: Margites, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE MARGITES
s: The Margites is attributed to Homer, though Suidas says that Pigres wrote it. Its fragments include descriptions of the foolish Margites and a proverb about the fox and the hedgehog.

l: Pigres, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE MARGITES
s: Pigres is identified by Suidas as a Carian of Halicarnassus and the brother of Artemisia, wife of Mausolus. He is said to have written the Margites attributed to Homer and the Battle of the Frogs and Mice.

l: Homer, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE MARGITES
s: The Margites is attributed to Homer in the account of Pigres.

l: Margites (character), Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE MARGITES
s: Margites knew many things but knew them all badly, and the gods had taught him neither to dig nor to plough nor any other skill. Though well grown up, he did not know whether his father or his mother had given him birth, and he would not lie with his wife because he feared she might report badly about him to her mother.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE CERCOPES
s: The Cercopes were two brothers, Passalus and Acmon, who lived on earth and practised every kind of knavery. They roamed widely, deceiving people with their cunning and relentless tricks. Their mother warned them to keep away from Black-bottom, identified as Heracles, and they were later said to have been turned to stone for trying to deceive Zeus.

l: Cercopes, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE CERCOPES
s: The Cercopes were two brothers, Passalus and Acmon, known for their cunning, lies, cheating, and knavery. They roamed far over the world deceiving people, and they were said to have been turned to stone for trying to deceive Zeus.

l: Passalus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE CERCOPES
s: Passalus was one of the two brothers called the Cercopes. He practised deceit and knavery with Acmon and was said to have been turned to stone for trying to deceive Zeus.

l: Acmon, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE CERCOPES
s: Acmon was one of the two brothers called the Cercopes. He practised deceit and knavery with Passalus and was said to have been turned to stone for trying to deceive Zeus.

l: Heracles, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE CERCOPES
s: Heracles was identified with Black-bottom, whom the mother of the Cercopes warned them to avoid.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE BATTLE OF FROGS AND MICE
s: The Battle of Frogs and Mice begins after Puff-jaw abandons Crumb-snatcher in the lake, causing the Mouse host to declare war on the Frogs. Both sides arm themselves with improvised weapons and armor, while Zeus and the gods watch rather than directly fight. Many Mice and Frogs are killed in the battle, and Slice-snatcher nearly destroys the Frogs before Zeus sends the crabs to rescue them. The crabs drive the Mice into flight, ending the one-day war at sunset.

l: The Battle of Frogs and Mice, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE BATTLE OF FROGS AND MICE
s: The battle begins because Puff-jaw abandons Crumb-snatcher in the lake and the Mice seek revenge. The Mice and Frogs fight fiercely with improvised weapons, but the crabs eventually drive the Mice into flight, ending the one-day war at sunset.

l: Mice, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE BATTLE OF FROGS AND MICE
s: The Mice become enraged after Crumb-snatcher drowns and assemble for war against the Frogs. They arm themselves with bean-pod greaves, ferret-skin breastplates, lamp shields, bronze needles, and pea-nut helmets, but flee when the crabs attack.

l: Frogs, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE BATTLE OF FROGS AND MICE
s: The Frogs gather in council, blame Puff-jaw for the quarrel, and arm themselves to fight the Mice. They suffer heavy losses during the battle and are rescued from near destruction when Zeus sends the crabs.

l: Crumb-snatcher, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE BATTLE OF FROGS AND MICE
s: Crumb-snatcher is a Mouse, the son of Bread-nibbler and Quern-licker, and he describes his preference for human foods and his fear of the ferret, hawk, and traps. After riding on Puff-jaw's back, he is abandoned in the lake when Puff-jaw dives from a water-snake and drowns. Later he fights to avenge the dead Mice, killing Leeky and Cabbage-climber before Croakperson kills him.

l: Puff-jaw, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE BATTLE OF FROGS AND MICE
s: Puff-jaw is the king of the Frogs and invites Crumb-snatcher to ride on his back to his house. When a water-snake appears, he dives and leaves Crumb-snatcher to drown, then denies killing him and urges the Frogs to destroy the Mice. Bread-nibbler later strikes him on the toes.

l: Zeus, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE BATTLE OF FROGS AND MICE
s: Zeus summons the gods to view the armies and asks who will aid the Frogs or the Mice. He watches the battle, becomes concerned when Slice-snatcher threatens to destroy the Frogs, frightens both armies with his thunderbolt, and finally sends the crabs to help the Frogs.

l: Athena, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE BATTLE OF FROGS AND MICE
s: Athena refuses to help the Mice because they have damaged her garlands, lamps, and sacred robe. She also refuses to help the Frogs because their loud calls once kept her awake, and she advises the gods to watch the battle instead.

l: gods, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE BATTLE OF FROGS AND MICE
s: The gods gather in heaven to watch the battle rather than directly assist either side. They agree with Athena's proposal to observe, and later the divine discussion leads to Zeus sending aid to the Frogs.

l: the lake, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE BATTLE OF FROGS AND MICE
s: The lake is where Crumb-snatcher drinks, rides with Puff-jaw, and drowns after Puff-jaw dives away. It becomes the setting for much of the battle, and its water is dyed with the blood of fallen fighters.

l: Bread-nibbler, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE BATTLE OF FROGS AND MICE
s: Bread-nibbler is Crumb-snatcher's father and becomes enraged when his son dies. He tells the Mice that he has already lost three sons to the ferret, a human trap, and Puff-jaw, urges them to arm themselves, and later strikes Puff-jaw on the toes.

l: Slice-snatcher, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE BATTLE OF FROGS AND MICE
s: Slice-snatcher is a powerful Mouse and the son of Gnawer, who is the son of Bread-stealer. He arms himself with split chestnut husks and threatens to destroy the Frogs, driving them toward the lake until Zeus intervenes.

l: the ferret, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE BATTLE OF FROGS AND MICE
s: The ferret is a dangerous enemy of the Mice. It has killed one of Bread-nibbler's sons and is feared because it can follow a Mouse into its hole; the Mice also make breastplates from the skin of a ferret they have flayed.

l: crabs, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE BATTLE OF FROGS AND MICE
s: The crabs are mailed, shell-covered creatures with curving claws, eight legs, feelers, and eyes that look behind them. Zeus sends them to aid the Frogs, and they nip off the Mice's tails, paws, and feet until the Mice flee.

l: the armor, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE BATTLE OF FROGS AND MICE
s: The Mice's armor consists of green bean-pod greaves, ferret-skin breastplates stretched on reeds, lamp-centre shields, bronze needle spears, and pea-nut helmets. The Frogs use mallow leaves for greaves, beet- and cabbage-leaf breastplates and shields, rush spears, and snail-shell helmets.

l: thunderbolt, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, THE BATTLE OF FROGS AND MICE
s: The thunderbolt is Zeus's formidable weapon. He casts it after Hera urges him to intervene, and it frightens both the Frogs and the Mice, though it does not stop the Mice from continuing to hope for victory.

l: Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, OF THE ORIGIN OF HOMER AND HESIOD, AND OF THEIR CONTEST
s: The unit recounts competing traditions about the origins, parentage, careers, and deaths of Homer and Hesiod. It describes a poetic contest between them at Chalcis, where Homer excelled in answering riddles and questions but Hesiod won the prize because he praised peace and husbandry. It also recounts Hesiod’s murder after a misinterpreted oracle and Homer’s later travels, performances, death at Ios, and burial there.

l: Homer, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, OF THE ORIGIN OF HOMER AND HESIOD, AND OF THEIR CONTEST
s: Homer is associated with Smyrna, Chios, Colophon, Ithaca, and other places, and differing accounts give him various parents and names, including Meles, Melesigenes, and Altes. He composed or performed the Iliad, Odyssey, Thebais, Epigoni, Margites, and Hymn to Apollo, traveled among Greek cities, received honors and gifts, and died at Ios after failing to understand a riddle about lice.

l: Hesiod, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, OF THE ORIGIN OF HOMER AND HESIOD, AND OF THEIR CONTEST
s: Hesiod is said to have come from Ascra and to have been the son of Dius and Pycimede in one genealogy. He competed with Homer at Chalcis, received the prize, dedicated his tripod to the Muses, and was later murdered at Oenoe after an oracle led him unknowingly to the sacred place of Nemean Zeus.

l: Pythia, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, OF THE ORIGIN OF HOMER AND HESIOD, AND OF THEIR CONTEST
s: The Pythia gave several responses concerning Homer, identifying him in one response with Ithaca, Telemachus, and Epicasta, and warning him in another that Ios would receive him dead and that he should beware the riddle of young children. She also foretold Hesiod’s fame and warned him against the pleasant grove of Nemean Zeus.

l: Chalcis, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, OF THE ORIGIN OF HOMER AND HESIOD, AND OF THEIR CONTEST
s: Chalcis in Euboea was the place where Homer and Hesiod were said to have met and competed at the funeral gathering for Amphidamas. Its leading men and Paneides judged the contest, and Hesiod was declared the winner.

l: Pytho, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, OF THE ORIGIN OF HOMER AND HESIOD, AND OF THEIR CONTEST
s: Homer went to Delphi to ask about his identity and country, and later visited Delphi again after losing the contest. He dedicated a silver bowl to Apollo there, while Hesiod went to Delphi to consult the oracle and dedicate the first fruits of his victory.

l: Ios, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, OF THE ORIGIN OF HOMER AND HESIOD, AND OF THEIR CONTEST
s: Ios was identified by an oracle as Homer’s mother’s country and as the place that would receive him dead. Homer eventually traveled there, stayed with Creophylus, died after falling in a clayey place, and was buried there.

l: Hellenes, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, OF THE ORIGIN OF HOMER AND HESIOD, AND OF THEIR CONTEST
s: The Hellenes admired Homer’s answers and called some of his verses golden. They favored Homer after hearing the finest passages from both poets, but Paneides overruled them and awarded the victory to Hesiod.

l: Homer-and-Hesiod contest, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, OF THE ORIGIN OF HOMER AND HESIOD, AND OF THEIR CONTEST
s: The contest took place at Chalcis and involved questions, riddling verses, mathematical calculation, moral answers, and recitations from the poets’ own works. Homer was said to excel in the exchanges, but Hesiod won because Paneides judged that a poet who promoted peace and husbandry deserved the prize over one who depicted war and slaughter.

l: Apollo’s oracle, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, OF THE ORIGIN OF HOMER AND HESIOD, AND OF THEIR CONTEST
s: The oracle associated Homer with Ithaca, Telemachus, and Epicasta, and another response directed him toward Ios while warning him about the riddle of young children. It also foretold Hesiod’s fame and warned him of death at the grove of Nemean Zeus; Hesiod misunderstood the warning and went to Oenoe in Locris.

l: tripod, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, OF THE ORIGIN OF HOMER AND HESIOD, AND OF THEIR CONTEST
s: Hesiod received a brazen tripod after being declared the winner at Chalcis. He dedicated it to the Muses of Helicon with an inscription stating that he had conquered divine Homer in a contest of song.

l: Homer's death, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, OF THE ORIGIN OF HOMER AND HESIOD, AND OF THEIR CONTEST
s: At Ios, Homer asked boys returning from fishing what they had caught, but they answered with a riddle about catching lice. When he understood the riddle and connected it with the oracle, he composed his own epitaph, slipped in a clayey place, and died three days later.

l: Hesiod’s murder, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, OF THE ORIGIN OF HOMER AND HESIOD, AND OF THEIR CONTEST
s: Hesiod stayed at Oenoe with Amphiphanes and Ganyetor, whose sister he was suspected of seducing. The young men killed him and cast his body into the sea; dolphins later brought it ashore, and the brothers were eventually destroyed by Zeus according to one account.

l: Hesiod's works and agrarian teaching, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, OF THE ORIGIN OF HOMER AND HESIOD, AND OF THEIR CONTEST
s: Hesiod recited verses describing the proper seasons for harvesting, ploughing, and sowing, and the need to work according to the seasons. Paneides preferred this teaching about peace and husbandry to Homer’s depiction of warfare.

l: poetic composition and performance, Hesiod, the Homeric Hymns, and Homerica, OF THE ORIGIN OF HOMER AND HESIOD, AND OF THEIR CONTEST
s: Homer and Hesiod are presented as traveling poets who composed, recited, and competed with epic and other verse. Homer performed the Margites, Thebais, Epigoni, Iliad, Odyssey, and Hymn to Apollo, while Hesiod recited agrarian and moral teaching and dedicated a tripod after his victory.

l: The Extant Odes of Pindar, The Extant Odes of Pindar, OLYMPIAN ODES. / I.
s: The ode celebrates Hieron of Syracuse, who won the horse-race at Olympia with his horse Pherenikos. It praises the Olympian games as the greatest of contests and recounts the story of Pelops, their founder. Pelops wins Hippodameia from Oinomaos with Poseidon’s aid, while the ode rejects the tale that Tantalos served Pelops’s flesh to the gods. The speaker praises Hieron’s justice, wealth, excellence, and hope for further glory.

l: Hieron of Syracuse, The Extant Odes of Pindar, OLYMPIAN ODES. / I.
s: Hieron is praised as the ruler of Sicily, where he governs with justice and gathers excellence of many kinds. He is celebrated for winning the Olympic horse-race with Pherenikos, and the speaker hopes to glorify him again in song.

l: Olympic games, The Extant Odes of Pindar, OLYMPIAN ODES. / I.
s: The Olympian games are presented as greater than all other contests and as the source of glorious song. They honor Pelops and offer lasting fame and a sweet tranquillity to those who win.

l: Pherenikos, The Extant Odes of Pindar, OLYMPIAN ODES. / I.
s: Pherenikos wins the horse-race at Pisa by running ungoaded along the banks of the Alpheos. His victory brings glory to Hieron, the Syracusans’ horse-loving king.

l: Pisa, The Extant Odes of Pindar, OLYMPIAN ODES. / I.
s: Pisa is the place where Pherenikos wins the horse-race and where the Olympian contests associated with Pelops are held.

l: Pelops, The Extant Odes of Pindar, OLYMPIAN ODES. / I.
s: Pelops is described as the founder of the Olympian games and as the beloved son of Poseidon. After being restored to mortal life, he wins Hippodameia as his bride, fathers six sons, and receives enduring honor beside the Alpheos.

l: Poseidon, The Extant Odes of Pindar, OLYMPIAN ODES. / I.
s: Poseidon loves Pelops and carries him to the house of Zeus. Later, after Pelops calls upon him, Poseidon provides a golden chariot and tireless winged horses that enable Pelops to overcome Oinomaos.

l: Tantalos, The Extant Odes of Pindar, OLYMPIAN ODES. / I.
s: Tantalos is said to have enjoyed exceptional honor from the guardians of Olympus but lost his fortune through excess and wrongdoing. He is punished with a great stone hanging above his head and is also condemned for stealing nectar and ambrosia from the immortals and giving them to mortals.

l: Hippodameia, The Extant Odes of Pindar, OLYMPIAN ODES. / I.
s: Hippodameia is the noble daughter of Oinomaos whom Pelops seeks to marry. Pelops wins her as his bride after overcoming Oinomaos in the contest.

l: Oinomaos, The Extant Odes of Pindar, OLYMPIAN ODES. / I.
s: Oinomaos delays giving Hippodameia in marriage and has already killed thirteen suitors. Pelops overcomes him with Poseidon’s aid and wins the maiden.

l: Pindar's ode, The Extant Odes of Pindar, OLYMPIAN ODES. / I.
s: The ode glorifies the Olympian games, Hieron’s victory, and the founding story of Pelops. It praises Hieron in an equestrian song and declares that the speaker’s Muse may proclaim an even greater glory for him in the future.

l: The Extant Odes of Pindar, The Extant Odes of Pindar, notes
s: The Olympic games were sacred to Zeus, and a horse won a race for Hieron. The notes discuss Pelops and the legend that his ivory shoulder replaced flesh eaten by the gods at Tantalos' table. Pindar rejects that legend and explains that people may believe an untrue tale because of its beautiful presentation, although such tales do not endure.

l: Olympic games, The Extant Odes of Pindar, notes
s: The Olympic games were sacred to Zeus.

l: Zeus, The Extant Odes of Pindar, notes
s: Zeus was the deity to whom the Olympic games were sacred.

l: legend of Pelops' ivory shoulder, The Extant Odes of Pindar, notes
s: The legend claimed that Pelops' ivory shoulder replaced his fleshly shoulder after the gods ate it at Tantalos' table. Pindar refuses to accept the legend because it would make the gods guilty of an infamous act.

l: Pelops, The Extant Odes of Pindar, notes
s: Pelops was associated with the legend that his ivory shoulder replaced a fleshly one eaten by the gods at Tantalos' table.

l: Graces, The Extant Odes of Pindar, notes
s: The Charites or Graces are goddesses of Grace or Beauty, often represented as three. Pindar uses them to explain why people may believe an untrue tale because of the beauty of its presentation.

l: Pindar, The Extant Odes of Pindar, notes
s: Pindar refuses to accept the legend of Pelops' ivory shoulder because it would make the gods guilty of an infamous act. He says that people may believe untrue tales for the beauty of their form, but such tales will not stand the test of time.

l: The Extant Odes of Pindar, The Extant Odes of Pindar, II.
s: The poem celebrates Theron of Akragas for winning the four-horse chariot-race and praises him as a god-fearing, generous, and civic-minded ruler. It honors Akragas and its ancestors, whose prosperity and fame are linked to their long-established settlement in Sicily. The poem invokes Zeus to protect Theron's native land and reflects on divine favor, changing fortune, and the fate of the dead. It describes judgment after death, punishment for the guilty, and a blessed existence for the virtuous before returning to praise Theron and his generosity.

l: Theron, The Extant Odes of Pindar, II.
s: Theron is celebrated as the winner of the four-horse chariot-race and as a righteous, god-fearing leader who supports Akragas. He is praised as exceptionally well-disposed toward friends and liberal in spirit, and his generosity is said to be too great for anyone to count.

l: Akragas, The Extant Odes of Pindar, II.
s: Akragas is called the eye of Sicily and the city supported by Theron's noble ancestors. Its people are praised for enduring long toil, gaining wealth and honor, and establishing a prosperous and famous city.

l: chariot-race victory, The Extant Odes of Pindar, II.
s: The victory was won by Theron's four-horse chariot, and it is the central occasion for the hymn. Victory is said to release the contestant from the pains of struggle and to bring honor and power.

l: Zeus, The Extant Odes of Pindar, II.
s: Zeus is invoked as lord of Olympus, the chief games, and the ford of Alpheos. He is asked to protect the native fields of Theron's people for their future sons, and he is described as judging the guilty souls beneath the earth.

l: afterlife judgment, The Extant Odes of Pindar, II.
s: The dead are judged for the sins committed in Zeus's realm, with the guilty souls paying penalties under the earth. The virtuous, especially those who have remained steadfast through repeated lives and avoided iniquity, travel to the tower of Kronos and enjoy a tearless life among the blessed.

l: wealth, The Extant Odes of Pindar, II.
s: The race's destiny is joined with heaven-sent prosperity, which brings wealth and honor and crowns inherited worth. Wealth made glorious by noble character gives a person power and inspires confidence, though fortune can later change for better or worse.

l: poetry and song, The Extant Odes of Pindar, II.
s: The speaker's songs and lyre proclaim Theron's victory, Akragas, and the deeds of heroic and divine figures. The poem presents its arrows or words as meaningful to the wise but requiring interpreters for the multitude, and it contrasts true natural artistry with empty learned chatter.

l: The Extant Odes of Pindar, The Extant Odes of Pindar, notes
s: The notes state that Theron traced his descent from the son of Polyneikes. They identify Pindar's views on future life as being especially preserved in surviving fragments of his Dirges. Pindar seems to have been influenced by Pythagoreanism in these ideas.

l: Theron, The Extant Odes of Pindar, notes
s: Theron traced his descent from the son of Polyneikes.

l: future life, The Extant Odes of Pindar, notes
s: Pindar's ideas about future life are found especially in the surviving fragments of his Dirges. These ideas seem to have been influenced by Pythagoreanism.

l: Pindar, The Extant Odes of Pindar, notes
s: Pindar expressed ideas about future life, particularly in the fragments of his Dirges that remain. He seems to have been influenced by Pythagoreanism.

l: The Extant Odes of Pindar, The Extant Odes of Pindar, III.
s: The ode celebrates Theron's victory in the chariot-race and his Olympian crown at Akragas. It was sung at the Theoxenia feast, which Theron gave in the name of the Dioskouroi, Tyndareus' sons. The poem recounts how Herakles brought the olive tree from the land of Ister for Zeus's precinct and established the Olympic games, including the fifth-year feast. It concludes that Theron and the Emmenidai have attained the furthest limit of mortal achievement through their victory and devotion to the Dioskouroi.

l: Theron, The Extant Odes of Pindar, III.
s: Theron is celebrated as the winner of the chariot-race and recipient of an Olympian crown. He gives the Theoxenia feast in the name of the Dioskouroi and is praised for honoring them with hospitality and pious observance.

l: Akragas, The Extant Odes of Pindar, III.
s: Akragas is honored in the hymn celebrating Theron's Olympian victory.

l: Theoxenia, The Extant Odes of Pindar, III.
s: The Theoxenia is a feast given by Theron in the name of the Dioskouroi to the other gods.

l: Dioskouroi, The Extant Odes of Pindar, III.
s: The Dioskouroi, identified as Kastor and Polydeukes and as the sons of Tyndareus, are invoked at the beginning of the ode. Theron and the Emmenidai honor them with tables of hospitality and observance of the rite of the blessed gods.

l: the Emmenidai, The Extant Odes of Pindar, III.
s: The Emmenidai are praised alongside Theron for receiving glory through the Tyndaridai of goodly steeds. They are especially devoted to the Dioskouroi and honor them with hospitality and pious rites.

l: Pisa, The Extant Odes of Pindar, III.
s: Pisa is said to bid the poet speak aloud, since songs of divine assignment come from her when the judge of the games places the olive glory upon a victor.

l: Herakles, The Extant Odes of Pindar, III.
s: Herakles fulfilled the behests of old by establishing the games and brought the olive tree from the land of Ister to Zeus's precinct. He also received help from Leto's horse-loving daughter during his quest for the golden-horned hind.

l: Zeus, The Extant Odes of Pindar, III.
s: The precinct of Zeus is the place to which Herakles brought the olive tree as a common shade and crown for valorous deeds. The games and their altars are associated with Zeus's worship.

l: the olive tree, The Extant Odes of Pindar, III.
s: The olive tree was brought by Herakles from the shadowy springs of Ister to serve as a memorial of Olympic triumphs. It was planted as a common shade and as a crown for valorous deeds.

l: the fifth-year feast, The Extant Odes of Pindar, III.
s: The fifth-year feast was ordained by Herakles beside the holy steeps of Alpheos as part of the great games.

l: the chariot-race, The Extant Odes of Pindar, III.
s: The chariot-race is the contest in which Theron won his celebrated victory and Olympian crown. The games also included the driving of the nimble car.

l: Theron's Olympian crown, The Extant Odes of Pindar, III.
s: Theron's Olympian crown is the subject of the hymn's celebration. It is associated with the pale-gleaming olive glory awarded at the games.

l: Olympic games, The Extant Odes of Pindar, III.
s: The Olympic games were established by Herakles after he sanctified the altars to his sire. They included contests between men and chariot driving, and were held with a fifth-year feast beside the Alpheos.

l: The Extant Odes of Pindar, The Extant Odes of Pindar, notes
s: The notes explain that the Dorian invasion of Peloponnesos was associated with Oxylos, who was said to be one of its leaders. Oxylos, of Elean descent but living in Aitolia, became king of Elis after the invasion. The judge at the Olympic games was thought to be descended from Oxylos or from an Aitolian who came with him. The Olympic games were held at the full moon in the middle of Hekatombaion, and Herakles was understood to have wanted to institute them at that favorable time.

l: Dorian invasion of Peloponnesos, The Extant Odes of Pindar, notes
s: The Dorian invasion of Peloponnesos was said to have been led in part by Oxylos.

l: Oxylos, The Extant Odes of Pindar, notes
s: Oxylos was said to be a leader of the Dorian invasion, of Elean descent but living in Aitolia. After the invasion, he became king of Elis.

l: Olympic games, The Extant Odes of Pindar, notes
s: The Olympic games were held in the middle of Hekatombaion, when the moon was full. Their judge was thought to be a descendant of Oxylos or of an Aitolian who came with him; the full moon was regarded as a season of good luck for their institution by Herakles.

l: The Extant Odes of Pindar, The Extant Odes of Pindar, IV.
s: This ode concerns Psaumis of Kamarina and his victory in the mule-chariot-race at Olympia in 452. It praises Psaumis for his horsemanship, hospitality, love of peace, and devotion to his city. The ode invokes Zeus, asks for favor in future prayers, and presents the victory as an enduring sign of valor. It was apparently written immediately after the victory for singing beneath the moon by Psaumis's returning companions.

l: Psaumis, The Extant Odes of Pindar, IV.
s: Psaumis won the mule-chariot-race at Olympia in 452 and was crowned with Pisan olive. He is praised as zealous in rearing horses, hospitable, peace-loving, devoted to Kamarina's welfare, and guileless.

l: Kamarina, The Extant Odes of Pindar, IV.
s: Kamarina is the city whose glory Psaumis seeks to raise through his victory.

l: Zeus, The Extant Odes of Pindar, IV.
s: Zeus is invoked as the hurler of unfaltering thunderbolts and the most high son of Kronos. He is asked to receive the band of triumph for the Olympian victory and to be gracious to the prayers associated with what shall come.

l: the mule-chariot-race, The Extant Odes of Pindar, IV.
s: The mule-chariot-race was introduced at Olympia in 500 and abolished in 444, according to Pausanias. Psaumis won the race in 452.

l: Psaumis's Olympian victory, The Extant Odes of Pindar, IV.
s: Psaumis's Olympian victory is presented as a lasting light and witness to far-prevailing valorous deeds, achieved with the aid of the Graces. It is celebrated through a song offered to Zeus.

l: the ode for Psaumis, The Extant Odes of Pindar, IV.
s: The ode for Psaumis is dated to his victory in 452 and is among the latest dated works of Pindar possessed by the text. It seems to have been written immediately after the victory to be sung that same night beneath the moon by Psaumis's companions as they returned to give thanks at Zeus's altar.

l: The Extant Odes of Pindar, The Extant Odes of Pindar, notes
s: The unit contains two footnotes. One directs the reader to the introduction to Pythian ix. The other suggests that Psaumis probably had grey hair.

l: Pythian ix, The Extant Odes of Pindar, notes
s: The introduction to Pythian ix is referenced in a footnote.

l: Psaumis, The Extant Odes of Pindar, notes
s: Psaumis is described as probably having grey hair.

l: The Extant Odes of Pindar, The Extant Odes of Pindar, V.
s: The ode celebrates Psaumis of Kamarina as winner of the mule-chariot race and was intended for performance after his return home. Psaumis is praised for honoring Kamarina through sacrifices, contests, and the public display of his Olympian victory, while also glorifying his father Akron and the restored city. The poem invokes Kamarina, Pallas, Zeus, and local rivers and places, and praises the city’s rebuilding and prosperity. It ends by asking Zeus to grant Psaumis a serene old age with his sons and advising contentment with wealth and good repute.

l: Psaumis, The Extant Odes of Pindar, V.
s: Psaumis is celebrated as the winner of the mule-chariot race and as the owner of an untiring car. He honors Kamarina through sacrifices and contests, glorifies his father Akron and the city, and is prayed for a serene old age with his sons.

l: Kamarina, The Extant Odes of Pindar, V.
s: Kamarina is called a new-peopled city and is praised as the city Psaumis helps make great. The ode asks Zeus to glorify it with the renown of brave men.

l: Zeus, The Extant Odes of Pindar, V.
s: Zeus is invoked as guardian of the city, seated above the clouds on the Kronian hill and associated with the Alpheos and Ida’s holy cave. The speaker prays that he will glorify Kamarina with the renown of brave men and grant Psaumis a serene old age.

l: Olympia, The Extant Odes of Pindar, V.
s: Olympia is represented through the gracious dwelling place of Oinomaos and Pelops and the Olympian victory celebrated in the ode. Psaumis returns from that sacred place and brings its victory honor to Kamarina.

l: Psaumis's Olympian victory, The Extant Odes of Pindar, V.
s: The mule-chariot race victory is the occasion of the ode. It is celebrated after Psaumis’s return to Kamarina and is presented as a source of honor for him, his father, and the city.

l: Olympian crown, The Extant Odes of Pindar, V.
s: The Olympian crown is the proud token of Psaumis’s fame that he consecrates to Kamarina. It represents his victory and is connected with the herald’s public glorification of his father and city.

l: Psaumis' untiring car, The Extant Odes of Pindar, V.
s: Psaumis’ untiring car is offered in connection with the sweet delight of his Olympian victory. It is part of the achievement by which he honors Kamarina.

l: five-day contests of games, The Extant Odes of Pindar, V.
s: Psaumis honors six twin altars in great feasts of the gods with sacrifices of oxen and five-day contests of games. These contests include competitions with horses, mules, and the steed of single frontlet.

l: mules, The Extant Odes of Pindar, V.
s: Mules take part in the five-day contests of games held in honor of the gods. Psaumis wins the mule-chariot race with them.

l: new city, The Extant Odes of Pindar, V.
s: The new city is identified with Kamarina, which had been destroyed by Gelo and restored nine years before the victory. Its rebuilding is associated with bringing the commonwealth from perplexity to light and with constructing steadfast dwellings.

l: citizens of Kamarina, The Extant Odes of Pindar, V.
s: The citizens of Kamarina are the people whose commonwealth is brought from perplexity to light as the city is rebuilt. The ode says that successful deeds and wisdom are approved by a person’s own townsfolk.

l: The Extant Odes of Pindar, The Extant Odes of Pindar, VI.
s: The ode celebrates Agesias of Syracuse, a citizen of both Syracuse and Stymphalos, who won the mule-chariot race at Olympia. It traces his descent from the Iamid clan through the story of Iamos, the prophetic son of Euadne and Apollo, whose descendants became renowned seers at Olympia. The poem praises Syracuse, Stymphalos, Hieron, and the gods associated with Agesias’s victory, and asks for continued prosperity for both of his communities.

l: Agesias of Syracuse, The Extant Odes of Pindar, VI.
s: Agesias, the son of Sostratos, won the mule-chariot race at Olympia. He was a citizen of Syracuse and Stymphalos, descended from the Iamid clan, and is praised as the subject of the triumphal ode.

l: Iamid clan, The Extant Odes of Pindar, VI.
s: The Iamid clan held hereditary priestly functions in Arcadia and at Olympia. Agesias descended from this clan, whose members became glorious among the Hellenes through their prophetic gifts.

l: Arcady, The Extant Odes of Pindar, VI.
s: Arcadia is identified as the region where the Iamid clan held hereditary priestly functions. It is also called the nurse of goodly men and is represented through Stymphalos and the Arcadian royal ancestry in the story.

l: Olympia, The Extant Odes of Pindar, VI.
s: Olympia is the place where Agesias won his victory in the mule-chariot race. It is also associated with the Iamid priestly tradition and with the oracle that Herakles was to establish at Zeus’s altar.

l: Syracuse, The Extant Odes of Pindar, VI.
s: Syracuse is the city where Agesias lived and of which he was a citizen. The ode calls him a joint founder of glorious Syracuse and asks that Syracuse and its ruler Hieron receive continued good fortune.

l: Stymphalos, The Extant Odes of Pindar, VI.
s: Stymphalos was Agesias’s other civic home and the place where the ode was sung by a chorus. It is called the mother-city of Arcadia, rich in flocks, and is compared with Syracuse as one of two anchors.

l: mule-chariot race, The Extant Odes of Pindar, VI.
s: The mule-chariot race was won by Agesias at Olympia. His mules had already won crowns there, and the poem presents their victory as a deed worthy of song.

l: Olympian victory, The Extant Odes of Pindar, VI.
s: The Olympian victory gives Agesias a claim to public praise and makes him treasurer to the prophetic altar of Zeus at Pisa. The ode treats the victory as an achievement won through labor rather than an unthreatening or insignificant deed.

l: the ode, The Extant Odes of Pindar, VI.
s: The ode celebrates Agesias’s victory, ancestry, and civic ties to Syracuse and Stymphalos. It recounts the birth and prophetic destiny of Iamos, praises Hieron and Syracuse, and closes by asking Poseidon to grant safe passage and prosperity.

l: Pitane, The Extant Odes of Pindar, VI.
s: Pitane, the nymph associated with the place of that name, lay with Poseidon and bore Euadne. The ode announces that it must travel toward Pitane and recounts her role in Iamos’s ancestry.

l: Poseidon, The Extant Odes of Pindar, VI.
s: Poseidon, the son of Kronos, lay with Pitane and became the grandfather of Iamos through Euadne. Iamos later called on Poseidon as his grandsire, and the poem finally asks Poseidon to grant a safe voyage and bless the song.

l: Euadne, The Extant Odes of Pindar, VI.
s: Euadne was born to Pitane and Poseidon and was reared by Aipytos. She conceived Iamos by Apollo, gave birth to him beneath a thicket, and left him there in her anguish.

l: Apollo, The Extant Odes of Pindar, VI.
s: Apollo was Euadne’s divine lover and the father of Iamos. He sent Eleutho and the Fates to assist at Iamos’s birth, and later answered Iamos with an infallible prophetic voice.

l: Iamos, The Extant Odes of Pindar, VI.
s: Iamos was the son of Euadne and Apollo and was nourished by two bright-eyed serpents with honey. As a young man he received a twofold prophetic treasure from Apollo and became the ancestor of the Iamidai, who were destined to be renowned among the Hellenes.

l: Iamos's prophetic oracle, The Extant Odes of Pindar, VI.
s: Iamos received prophecy from Apollo at the rock of Kronion. He was first to heed Apollo’s truthful voice, and after Herakles founded the Olympic festival and games, he was to establish another oracle at Zeus’s altar.

l: Hieron of Syracuse, The Extant Odes of Pindar, VI.
s: Hieron ruled Syracuse and Ortygia with a righteous sceptre and true counsels. He honored Demeter, her daughter’s festival, and Aetnaean Zeus, and was known for song and lute.

l: the chorus, The Extant Odes of Pindar, VI.
s: A chorus in Stymphalos sang the ode. It is urged to proclaim Hera, mention Syracuse and Ortygia, and correctly understand and perform the song.

l: the Muses' song, The Extant Odes of Pindar, VI.
s: The Muses’ sweet voice is invoked as a witness to the poet’s praise of Agesias. Their song travels from home to home with the triumphal ode and supplies the harmonious speech that celebrates the victor.

l: Iamos's birth, The Extant Odes of Pindar, VI.
s: Iamos was born beneath a thicket after Euadne removed her pitcher and scarlet girdle. Eleutho and the Fates assisted, and two divinely directed serpents nourished the abandoned child with honey.

l: Syracuse's foundation, The Extant Odes of Pindar, VI.
s: Syracuse is described as having been jointly founded by an ancestor of Agesias who came with Archias and the first colonists. This ancestral connection contributes to Agesias’s praise as a Syracusan.

l: The Extant Odes of Pindar, The Extant Odes of Pindar, VII.
s: This unit presents a victory ode for Diagoras of Rhodes, who won the boxing-match at Olympia and returned home celebrated. It praises Rhodes, its three cities, its divine origins through Helios and Rhodos, and the noble lineage of Diagoras and the Eratidai. The poem recounts Tlepolemos's accidental killing of Likymnios, his consultation of Apollo's oracle, and the founding traditions of Rhodes. It also lists Diagoras's victories at Olympia and other Greek games and asks Zeus to honor him and his city.

l: Diagoras of Rhodes, The Extant Odes of Pindar, VII.
s: Diagoras, of the Eratidai family of Ialysos, won the boxing-match at Olympia and is celebrated in this ode. He also won twice at Olympia, four times at Isthmos, twice at Nemea, twice at Athens, and at several other games including six victories at Aigina.

l: Rhodes, The Extant Odes of Pindar, VII.
s: Rhodes is praised as a sea-girt island, child of Aphrodite and bride of Helios, and as the land divided among Kameiros, Ialysos, and Lindos. Its traditions include the emergence of the island from the sea, the rule of Helios, and the divine gifts of gold and handicraft.

l: Pindaric victory ode, The Extant Odes of Pindar, VII.
s: The ode sends the Muses' nectar to celebrate men who win at Pytho or Olympia. In this unit it accompanies Diagoras home, glorifies his boxing victory and lineage, and celebrates Rhodes and its ancestral myths.

l: boxing-match, The Extant Odes of Pindar, VII.
s: The boxing-match at Olympia was won by Diagoras. His victory provides the central occasion for the ode and earns him praise and glory among citizens and strangers.

l: Tlepolemos, The Extant Odes of Pindar, VII.
s: Tlepolemos, regarded as the founder of Rhodes and leader of the Tirynthians, accidentally slew Likymnios in Tiryns during a fit of anger. After consulting an oracle, he was associated with the colonization of Rhodes and received honor in games as the island's tutelary hero.

l: Eratidai, The Extant Odes of Pindar, VII.
s: The Eratidai were the former royal dynasty of Ialysos, whose kingly power had been extinct for two hundred years but whose family remained pre-eminent. Diagoras belonged to this family, and the city rejoices with the Eratidai in his success.

l: Helios, The Extant Odes of Pindar, VII.
s: Helios, the god who gives light and the father of the keen rays of day, was left without a land allotment because he was elsewhere when the gods divided the earth. Rhodes rose from the sea for him, and after lying with Rhodos he fathered seven sons, including the ancestors of Kameiros, Ialysos, and Lindos.

l: Olympic games, The Extant Odes of Pindar, VII.
s: The Olympic Games are among the contests whose winners receive the ode's praise. Diagoras won twice at Olympia, and the poem asks Zeus to glorify the customary hymn for an Olympian winner.

l: Olympian victory, The Extant Odes of Pindar, VII.
s: Diagoras's Olympian victory was achieved in boxing and is celebrated as a source of honor for him, his family, and Rhodes. The ode asks Zeus to grant him continued recognition from citizens and strangers.

l: Zeus, The Extant Odes of Pindar, VII.
s: Zeus is the father of Athene and is said to have rained golden snow upon Rhodes when Athene was born. He also caused a yellow cloud to rain gold on the Rhodians and is asked to glorify Diagoras and the Olympian victory hymn from Mount Atabyrios.

l: Athene, The Extant Odes of Pindar, VII.
s: Athene sprang from the crown of Zeus's head beneath Hephaistos's bronze-wrought axe and cried out so loudly that Heaven and Earth trembled. She received an altar from the sons of Helios and gave the Rhodians superiority in every art of handicraft.

l: The Extant Odes of Pindar, The Extant Odes of Pindar, VIII.
s: The unit celebrates Alkimedon of Aigina, who won the boys’ wrestling match at Olympia in 460 B.C. His victory is connected with the glory of his brother Timosthenes, his trainer Melesias, and the Blepsiad clan. The ode praises Aigina’s reputation for justice and hospitality and recalls Aiakos’s role in the building of Troy. It asks Zeus to grant continuing honor, health, and prosperity to Alkimedon’s family and community.

l: Alkimedon, The Extant Odes of Pindar, VIII.
s: Alkimedon is presented as a beautiful boy who won the Olympic wrestling match without bringing shame upon his appearance. By winning, he proclaimed Aigina as his homeland, gained glory for his family, and renewed his grandfather’s strength in old age.

l: Timosthenes, The Extant Odes of Pindar, VIII.
s: Timosthenes is Alkimedon’s brother and had won a victory at the Nemean games. Destiny assigned both brothers to Zeus, who made Timosthenes glorious at Nemea and Alkimedon a winner at Olympia.

l: Zeus, The Extant Odes of Pindar, VIII.
s: Zeus is invoked as the wielder of white lightning, the guardian of Timosthenes’ and Alkimedon’s house, and the god who grants answers concerning human excellence. He is also credited with granting Olympic glory to the family and is asked to preserve its honor and protect it from disease.

l: Aiakos, The Extant Odes of Pindar, VIII.
s: Aiakos was called by Apollo and Poseidon to help build the wall of Troy. After three fiery-eyed dragons attacked the new wall, Apollo interpreted the surviving dragon as a sign that Troy would be taken through Aiakos’ descendants, including Telamon and Neoptolemos.

l: Olympia, The Extant Odes of Pindar, VIII.
s: Olympia is called the mother of gold-crowned contests and the queen of truth. The speaker asks its tree-clad precinct by the Alpheos to receive Alkimedon’s triumph and crown.

l: Aigina, The Extant Odes of Pindar, VIII.
s: Aigina is described as a sea-defended land and a pillar of support for strangers from every region. It is praised as the Dorian homeland of Alkimedon and for honoring Themis, who presides over justice and the protection of strangers.

l: wrestling match, The Extant Odes of Pindar, VIII.
s: The wrestling match at Olympia was won by Alkimedon while he was still a boy. His victory defeated four successive opponents and transferred to them the disgrace of an unwelcome, unhonored return.

l: Alkimedon's Olympic victory, The Extant Odes of Pindar, VIII.
s: Alkimedon’s Olympic victory took place in 460 B.C. and was celebrated in an ode apparently intended for performance in a procession to Zeus’s altar on the night of the victory.

l: glory, The Extant Odes of Pindar, VIII.
s: Fame and honor are presented as gifts granted differently to different people through divine favor and as the proper reward for noble deeds. The ode asks that honor continue to come to Alkimedon’s house, whose clan has received six crowns from the wreathed games, and that its glory be shared without envy or discontent.

l: The Extant Odes of Pindar, The Extant Odes of Pindar, IX.
s: The ode celebrates Epharmostos of Opous as victor in the wrestling-match at Olympia and recounts his other athletic successes. It praises Opous and the Lokrians through myths of Zeus, Protogeneia, Pyrrha, Deukalion, Lokros, Menoitios, Patroklos, and Achilles. It also tells of Herakles' struggle with gods at Pylos and concludes that Epharmostos' victory arose from natural and divinely granted prowess, marked by his crowning of the altar of Aias Oileus.

l: Epharmostos, The Extant Odes of Pindar, IX.
s: Epharmostos of Opous won the wrestling-match at Olympia. He also gained victories at the Isthmus, Nemea, Argos, Athens, Marathon, the assembly of Lykaian Zeus, Pellene, the tomb of Iolaos, and Eleusis, and at the end he crowned the altar of Aias Oileus.

l: Opous, The Extant Odes of Pindar, IX.
s: Opous is the famous city of Epharmostos and is praised as a city of beautiful trees. Its glory is celebrated along with that of its son Epharmostos.

l: wrestling-match at Olympia, The Extant Odes of Pindar, IX.
s: The wrestling-match at Olympia was won by Epharmostos. His victory is the occasion for the ode's praise.

l: Pindar, The Extant Odes of Pindar, IX.
s: Pindar presents himself as sending song to illuminate the city of his friends and to praise Epharmostos. He recalls Epharmostos' victories and invokes the Muses' power to celebrate them.

l: Aias Oileus, The Extant Odes of Pindar, IX.
s: Aias Oileus is named as the tutelar hero whose altar Epharmostos crowned at the feast.

l: Zeus, The Extant Odes of Pindar, IX.
s: Zeus is praised as the god of the red or bickering lightning-flash. He brought about the ebb of the flood and fathered the child born to the daughter of Opöeis, and by his decree Pyrrha and Deukalion established the city of Protogeneia.

l: Lokrians, The Extant Odes of Pindar, IX.
s: The Lokrians are associated with Opous, their mother city of beautiful trees. Their ancestral story traces them through Lokros, the daughter of Opöeis, and the child begotten by Zeus.

l: Herakles, The Extant Odes of Pindar, IX.
s: At Pylos, Herakles wielded his club against Poseidon, Phoibos, and Hades, who opposed him with a trident, a silver bow, and a staff. The ode then warns against speaking evil of the gods.

l: Protogeneia, The Extant Odes of Pindar, IX.
s: Protogeneia is named as a city to which the song should turn after the account of conflict among immortals. Zeus decreed that Pyrrha and Deukalion first settled there.

l: Pyrrha, The Extant Odes of Pindar, IX.
s: Pyrrha came down from Parnassos with Deukalion and first established a home in the city of Protogeneia. Together they made a race into one people from stones without marriage.

l: Deukalion, The Extant Odes of Pindar, IX.
s: Deukalion came down from Parnassos with Pyrrha and settled in Protogeneia. With Pyrrha, he made a race from stones after the great flood.

l: Lokros, The Extant Odes of Pindar, IX.
s: Lokros received the daughter of Opöeis after Zeus had lain with her in Mainalos. Because Lokros was childless, Zeus's son was brought to him, and the child later became a ruler of a city and people.

l: flood of Zeus, The Extant Odes of Pindar, IX.
s: A mighty flood once swept over the dark earth, but Zeus caused the waters suddenly to ebb. From the survivors came the ancestors of the people described in the ode.

l: Menoitios, The Extant Odes of Pindar, IX.
s: Menoitios, the son of Aktor and Aigina, was honored above the other settlers who came to Lokros. He was the father of Patroklos.

l: Patroklos, The Extant Odes of Pindar, IX.
s: Patroklos went with the Atreidai to Teuthras and stood beside Achilles when Telephos routed the Danaoi. His courage was thereby shown, and Achilles later persuaded him not to stand far from his conquering spear in battle.

l: Achilles, The Extant Odes of Pindar, IX.
s: Achilles fought beside Patroklos and recognized his strength. He persuaded Patroklos to remain near him in murderous battle rather than take a distant position.

l: Olympia, The Extant Odes of Pindar, IX.
s: Olympia is the place where Epharmostos won the wrestling victory. Its crowns are described as among the choicest honors that glorify Opous.

l: altar of Aias Oileus, The Extant Odes of Pindar, IX.
s: The altar of Aias Oileus is the altar crowned by Epharmostos at the feast after his victory.

l: natural talent and divinely granted prowess, The Extant Odes of Pindar, IX.
s: The ode declares that valour and wisdom come to men by divine fate and that natural ability is best. Epharmostos is proclaimed to have been born deft-handed, nimble-limbed, and bright-eyed with valour, while achievements made without God should be kept silent.

l: The Extant Odes of Pindar, The Extant Odes of Pindar, X.
s: The ode concerns Agesidamos of Epizephyrian Lokris, son of Archestratos, who won the boys' boxing-match. It was to be sung at Olympia on the night after his victory, while a longer ode was promised for the later celebration in his Italian home. Pindar promises to honor Agesidamos with sweet songs and to remember the Lokrians' colony in the West. The poem praises the glory of Olympian winners and invokes the Muses to sing of a noble and valiant people.

l: Agesidamos of Epizephyrian Lokris, The Extant Odes of Pindar, X.
s: Agesidamos, son of Archestratos, won the boys' boxing-match. Pindar promises to place a glory of sweet strains upon his crown of golden olive and to write a longer ode for the celebration of his victory in his Italian home.

l: Olympia, The Extant Odes of Pindar, X.
s: The ode was to be sung at Olympia on the night after Agesidamos' victory. Olympian winners are said to have ample glory.

l: Olympic boxing-match, The Extant Odes of Pindar, X.
s: Agesidamos won the boys' boxing-match. His boxing is the achievement that Pindar promises to celebrate in song.

l: victory, The Extant Odes of Pindar, X.
s: Agesidamos' victory was to be celebrated at Olympia on the following night and later in his Italian home. The victory is associated with a crown of golden olive and the glory of Olympian winners.

l: music and poetry, The Extant Odes of Pindar, X.
s: The text says that honey-voiced songs are due when someone fares well through labor. Pindar promises sweet strains for Agesidamos and calls on the Muses to join in the song of triumph.

l: glory, The Extant Odes of Pindar, X.
s: The poem describes ample glory as stored for Olympian winners. Pindar promises to place such glory in sweet strains upon Agesidamos' crown of golden olive.

l: The Extant Odes of Pindar, The Extant Odes of Pindar, XI.
s: The unit is a delayed victory ode by Pindar for Agesidamos of Epizephyrian Lokris, who won the boys' boxing-match at Olympia. Pindar asks the Muse and Truth to release him from blame for having forgotten his promise, and he celebrates Agesidamos, his trainer Ilas, and the Lokrian people. The poem recounts Herakles' foundation of the Olympic games at Pisa, including the establishment of the Altis, the Hill of Kronos, and the first Olympiad. It ends by praising the value of song in preserving a victor's fame.

l: Agesidamos of Epizephyrian Lokris, The Extant Odes of Pindar, XI.
s: Agesidamos, son of Archestratos, won the boys' boxing-match at Olympia. Pindar praises his beauty, natural gifts, and victory, and says that song and music will preserve his fame.

l: Epizephyrian Lokris, The Extant Odes of Pindar, XI.
s: Epizephyrian Lokris is described as a western Lokrian city where Truth dwells. Its people honor Kalliope and mailed Ares, and Pindar celebrates the city's noble race.

l: Pindar, The Extant Odes of Pindar, XI.
s: Pindar admits that he had forgotten his promise to compose a sweet strain for Agesidamos. He seeks to repay the debt with usury by composing a victory song for Agesidamos and the Lokrians.

l: Olympic boxing-match, The Extant Odes of Pindar, XI.
s: The boys' boxing-match at Olympia was won by Agesidamos of Epizephyrian Lokris.

l: Olympia, The Extant Odes of Pindar, XI.
s: Olympia is the place where Pindar saw Agesidamos victorious beside the altar. It is also the site of the games founded by Herakles and of the first Olympiad.

l: Zeus, The Extant Odes of Pindar, XI.
s: Zeus gives the ordinances that inspire Pindar to sing of the Olympic games. Herakles dedicates the sacred grove to Zeus, and Zeus is celebrated as the loud-pealing god of thunder, lightning, and victory.

l: Herakles, The Extant Odes of Pindar, XI.
s: Herakles founded the Olympic games after killing Kleatos and Eurytos and forcing Augeas to pay for service done. He gathered his host and booty at Pisa, established the Altis and its boundaries, honored the Alpheos and the twelve greatest gods, and instituted the fifth-year feast.

l: Olympic games, The Extant Odes of Pindar, XI.
s: The Olympic games were founded by Herakles beside the ancient tomb of Pelops. Their first contests included foot-racing, wrestling, boxing, chariot racing, javelin, and stone-throwing.

l: Pelops, The Extant Odes of Pindar, XI.
s: The Olympic games were founded by Herakles beside the ancient tomb of Pelops.

l: Augeas, The Extant Odes of Pindar, XI.
s: Augeas is portrayed as the guest-betraying and tyrannous king of the Epeans. Herakles demanded payment for service done; after conflict, Augeas saw his city destroyed and eventually fell into captivity, escaping neither confusion nor sudden death.

l: Pisa, The Extant Odes of Pindar, XI.
s: Herakles gathered his host and all the booty at Pisa after his victories. There he established the sacred grove and the surrounding arrangements for the games.

l: Altis, The Extant Odes of Pindar, XI.
s: Herakles fenced the Altis and marked its boundaries in a clear space. He dedicated it as a sacred grove to Zeus.

l: hill of Kronos, The Extant Odes of Pindar, XI.
s: Herakles named the previously nameless hill the Hill of Kronos. At the time when Oinomaos was king, it was described as being sprinkled with much snow.

l: first Olympiad, The Extant Odes of Pindar, XI.
s: The first Olympiad is associated with the fifth-year feast and the victories established after Herakles founded the games. Its contests were won by Oionos in the foot-race, Echemos in wrestling, Doryklos in boxing, Samos in the four-horse chariot, Phrastor with the javelin, and Enikeus in stone-throwing.

l: victory song, The Extant Odes of Pindar, XI.
s: The victory song repays Pindar's delayed obligation to Agesidamos and celebrates his victory, his people, and his trainer Ilas. Pindar presents song as necessary because an honorable deed that goes unsung leaves its performer with only brief gladness for his toil.

l: The Extant Odes of Pindar, The Extant Odes of Pindar, XII.
s: The unit concerns Ergoteles of Himera, who won the long foot-race at Olympia after leaving Knosos because of civil dissension and becoming a citizen of Himera. It describes Fortune as governing ships, wars, councils, and the uncertain outcomes of human hopes. Ergoteles also won twice at Pytho and once at Isthmos, bringing glory to the Sicilian hot springs where the nymphs bathe. The ode's prayer asks Fortune to protect Himera, in apparent reference to the expulsion of Thrasydaios of Akragas by the Himeraeans.

l: Ergoteles, The Extant Odes of Pindar, XII.
s: Ergoteles was a native of Knosos who was driven from his country by civil dissension and became a citizen of Himera. He won the long foot-race at Olympia, twice at Pytho, and at Isthmos, gaining glory for the land that had become his own.

l: Fortune, The Extant Odes of Pindar, XII.
s: Fortune is addressed as the daughter of Zeus the Deliverer and the saviour of Himera. She is said to pilot swift ships and to govern fierce wars, councils, and the uncertain outcomes of human hopes.

l: Himera, The Extant Odes of Pindar, XII.
s: Himera is prayed to be kept safe by Fortune. It naturalized Ergoteles as a citizen after he left Knosos, and its hot springs are glorified by his victories.

l: Knosos, The Extant Odes of Pindar, XII.
s: Knosos was Ergoteles's native city. He left it after civil dissension drove him from his country.

l: Crete, The Extant Odes of Pindar, XII.
s: Crete was Ergoteles's homeland through his origin at Knosos. The Cretans are said to have kept aloof from the Panhellenic games.

l: Sicily, The Extant Odes of Pindar, XII.
s: Sicily was where Ergoteles came after leaving Crete. He was naturalized as a citizen of Himera there.

l: Himeraeans, The Extant Odes of Pindar, XII.
s: The Himeraeans expelled the tyrant Thrasydaios of Akragas in the year before the ode's date.

l: Thrasydaios of Akragas, The Extant Odes of Pindar, XII.
s: Thrasydaios of Akragas was a tyrant whom the Himeraeans expelled.

l: civil dissension, The Extant Odes of Pindar, XII.
s: Civil dissension compelled Ergoteles to leave Knosos and his native country.

l: expulsion of Thrasydaios, The Extant Odes of Pindar, XII.
s: The expulsion of Thrasydaios occurred when the Himeraeans removed the tyrant from Akragas in the year before the ode's date. The prayer to Fortune appears to refer especially to this event.

l: long foot-race, The Extant Odes of Pindar, XII.
s: The long foot-race was won by Ergoteles at Olympia.

l: Olympic victory, The Extant Odes of Pindar, XII.
s: Ergoteles's Olympic victory was his win in the long foot-race at Olympia, where he received a crown.

l: Pythian victories, The Extant Odes of Pindar, XII.
s: Ergoteles won two Pythian victories at Pytho.

l: Isthmian victory, The Extant Odes of Pindar, XII.
s: Ergoteles won an Isthmian victory at Isthmos.

l: Olympia, The Extant Odes of Pindar, XII.
s: Olympia was the place where Ergoteles won a crown in the long foot-race.

l: Pytho, The Extant Odes of Pindar, XII.
s: Pytho was the site of two victories by Ergoteles.

l: Isthmos, The Extant Odes of Pindar, XII.
s: Isthmos was the site of a victory by Ergoteles.

l: chance, The Extant Odes of Pindar, XII.
s: Chance brings unexpected outcomes to human beings, sometimes thwarting delight and sometimes turning sorrowful struggle into profound happiness. No person receives from God a sure sign of what will happen, and divinations of the future are blind.

l: The Extant Odes of Pindar, The Extant Odes of Pindar, XIII.
s: The unit celebrates Xenophon of Corinth, who in 464 B.C. won the Stadion race and the Pentathlon at Olympia. It praises Corinth, its athletic traditions, and the Oligaithidai, while listing Xenophon’s and his family’s victories at several Greek games. It also recounts the Corinthian hero Bellerophon’s divine-guided taming of Pegasos and his exploits against the Amazons, the Solymoi, and Chimaira. The ode concludes by asking Zeus to grant honour and prosperity to Xenophon and his family.

l: Xenophon of Corinth, The Extant Odes of Pindar, XIII.
s: Xenophon won the Stadion race and the Pentathlon at Olympia in 464 B.C. He also had two victories at the Isthmian games and at Nemea, and the ode celebrates his return to Corinth with his Olympic crown.

l: Corinth, The Extant Odes of Pindar, XIII.
s: Corinth is praised as a happy city, the portal of Isthmian Poseidon and a nursery of splendid youth. Its traditions of athletic excellence, invention, music, warfare, and heroic ancestry are celebrated.

l: Stadion race, The Extant Odes of Pindar, XIII.
s: The Stadion race was the short foot-race of about a furlong or 220 yards. Xenophon won it at Olympia in 464 B.C.

l: The Pentathlon, The Extant Odes of Pindar, XIII.
s: The Pentathlon consisted of the Jump, throwing the Disk, throwing the Javelin, the Foot-race, and Wrestling. Xenophon won the Pentathlon at Olympia, probably by winning at least three of its five contests.

l: Isthmian Games, The Extant Odes of Pindar, XIII.
s: Xenophon had two victories at the Isthmian games, where parsley wreaths were placed on his head before the people. The Oligaithidai also achieved many victories at the games of Poseidon between the seas.

l: Bellerophon, The Extant Odes of Pindar, XIII.
s: Bellerophon is presented as a Corinthian hero who obtained and mastered Pegasos with divine assistance. He used the winged horse against the Amazons, the Solymoi, and Chimaira, though the ode declines to describe his later fate.

l: Glaukos, The Extant Odes of Pindar, XIII.
s: Glaukos came from Lydia, and the Danaoi feared him. He declared that his father ruled in Peirene and possessed a rich inheritance of land and a palace.

l: Pegasos, The Extant Odes of Pindar, XIII.
s: Pegasos was the winged horse whom Bellerophon longed to bridle at Peirene’s spring. After Athene provided a golden bit and instructed Bellerophon through a dream, Pegasos was mastered and later found a home in the ancient stalls of Zeus at Olympus.

l: Zeus, The Extant Odes of Pindar, XIII.
s: Zeus is addressed as the sovereign of Olympia and as the father of Athene. He is asked to protect Corinth, preserve Xenophon’s favourable fortune, and grant honour and prosperity to the Oligaithidai.

l: Pallas, The Extant Odes of Pindar, XIII.
s: Athene appeared to Bellerophon in a dream as the maiden wielding the shadowy aegis. She gave him a golden bit for Pegasos and directed him to sacrifice and build an altar to her as queen of steeds.

l: Oligaithidai, The Extant Odes of Pindar, XIII.
s: The Oligaithidai were the clan to which Xenophon belonged. They were associated with victories at the Isthmian and Nemean games and with many other athletic successes throughout Hellas.

l: Peirene, The Extant Odes of Pindar, XIII.
s: Peirene was the spring where Bellerophon attempted to bridle Pegasos. Glaukos also said that his father ruled in the city of Peirene and possessed a rich heritage there.

l: victory at Olympia in 464 B.C., The Extant Odes of Pindar, XIII.
s: In 464 B.C., Xenophon won both the Stadion race and the Pentathlon at Olympia. The victory was celebrated in an ode thought to have been sung during his public entrance into Corinth.

l: Bellerophon's taming of Pegasos, The Extant Odes of Pindar, XIII.
s: Bellerophon’s taming of Pegasos began when Athene appeared to him in a dream and gave him a golden bit. After he followed the seer’s instructions and made the sacrifice, he placed the bit around Pegasos’s jaw and mastered the winged horse.

l: The Extant Odes of Pindar, The Extant Odes of Pindar, XIV.
s: The ode concerns Asopichos of Orchomenos, who won the boys' short foot-race in the Olympic games in 476 B.C. It was probably sung by a chorus of boys at Orchomenos, likely in the temple of the Graces. The poem praises the Graces and asks Echo to carry news of Asopichos's victory to his dead father in Persephone's realm.

l: Asopichos, The Extant Odes of Pindar, XIV.
s: Asopichos is celebrated as the winner of the boys' short foot-race for Orchomenos. In Pisa's valley, he crowned his boyish hair with garlands from the glorious games, bringing honour to his father.

l: Orchomenos, The Extant Odes of Pindar, XIV.
s: Orchomenos is the city of Asopichos and is described as the lusty land of goodly steeds that drink the waters of Kephisos. Its home, the Minyai's ancient race, is declared the winner through Asopichos's Olympic victory.

l: boys' short foot-race, The Extant Odes of Pindar, XIV.
s: The boys' short foot-race was won by Asopichos of Orchomenos.
